Content:
Each elementary matrix [MATH: E] is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as [MATH: E].
To illustrate, let's consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|0; 4|1]]
To find the inverse of [MATH: E,] we proceed as follows:

Content:
Step 1: Write down [MATH: \color{blue}E] and the identity matrix [MATH: I_2] side-by-side, as shown below:
[MATH: 1|0|1|0; 4|1|0|1]

Content:
Step 2: Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation [MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.] We apply the operation to the entire row (not only the left part):

Content:
[MATH: [E|I_{2}]|= [1|0|1|0; 4|1|0|1]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|0|1|0; 0|1|− 4|1]; = [I_{2}|E^{− 1}]]

Content:
The matrix [MATH: E^{-1}] is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
[MATH: [1|0; − 4|1]]

Content:
We can work out the inverse of all elementary [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrices in a similar way.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An elementary matrix is a matrix that can be obtained from the identity matrix by applying only one elementary row operation.

Content:
For example, starting with the [MATH: 2 \times 2] identity matrix [MATH: [1|0; 0|1]] we can apply a single elementary row operation to get any of the matrices below:

Content:
[MATH: [0|1; 1|0]]

Content:
- [MATH: E_1] is obtained from [MATH: I_2] by applying the row operation [MATH: R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.]
- [MATH: E_2] is obtained from [MATH: I_2] by applying the row operation [MATH: R_1:=2R_1.]
- [MATH: E_3] is obtained from [MATH: I_2] by applying the row operation [MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-7)R_1.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying an Elementary 2x2 Matrix

Example Prompt:
Is
[MATH: E = [1|0; − 5|1]]
an elementary matrix?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

The given matrix [MATH: E] is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from [MATH: I_2] by applying the elementary row operation [MATH: R_2:= R_2+(-5) R_1,] as follows:

[MATH: I_{2}|= [1|0; 0|1]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 5)R_{1}; ∼[1|0; − 5|1]; = E]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Inverse of an Elementary Matrix

Content:
Each elementary matrix [MATH: E] is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as [MATH: E].
To illustrate, let's consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|0; 4|1]]
To find the inverse of [MATH: E,] we proceed as follows:

Content:
Step 1: Write down [MATH: \color{blue}E] and the identity matrix [MATH: I_2] side-by-side, as shown below:
[MATH: 1|0|1|0; 4|1|0|1]

Content:
Step 2: Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation [MATH: R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.] We apply the operation to the entire row (not only the left part):

Content:
[MATH: [E|I_{2}]|= [1|0|1|0; 4|1|0|1]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|0|1|0; 0|1|− 4|1]; = [I_{2}|E^{− 1}]]

Content:
The matrix [MATH: E^{-1}] is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
[MATH: [1|0; − 4|1]]

Content:
We can work out the inverse of all elementary [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrices in a similar way.

EXPLANATION

[MATH: [E|I]|= [1|0|1|0; 0|(2)/(5)|0|1]|R_{2}:=(5)/(2)R_{2}; ∼[1|0|1|0; 0|1|0|(5)/(2)]]

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
[MATH: [1|0; 0|(5)/(2)]]
